France-Germany 10-year spread (ECB, monthly)
items.degraded: Monthly averages from the ECB instead of daily Banque de France yields: a daily move, a stop or a target inside the month is invisible, and the latest value is up to five weeks old. New book trades switch to the daily series automatically once Webstat succeeds; open trades keep the series they were filled on. A trade requested on a monthly series fills at the next month's average, dated the 1st, once the ECB publishes it after that month ends. No free daily French 10-year source works from GitHub Actions (checked 30 Oct 2026): the ECB's public market-data set has no country bond yields, Eurostat's daily series (irt_lt_mcby_d) is no longer published, the Bundesbank's yields by ISIN cover German securities only, FRED has only the OECD monthly figure, and AFT, CNBC and Stooq refuse automated requests.

items.name: 2027 budget bills (PLF and PLFSS 2027)
items.what: The 2027 finance and social-security bills presented on 1 October 2026: about 54 billion euros of consolidation, of which 43 billion of new measures (including a freeze of the civil-service pay index and of basic pensions except the lowest).
items.claim: The public deficit falls from 5.4% of GDP in 2026 to 5.0% in 2027, with growth of 1.0% in 2027 after 0.5% and inflation of 1.8%.
items.assessment: The 1.0% growth assumption looks optimistic; most forecasters are one to three tenths lower and downside risks dominate. The spending path is achievable only if every measure is adopted, which depends on Parliament passing the bills.

items.name: Pension reform suspension and the 2027 pension freeze
items.what: The 2026 social-security financing law suspended the 2023 pension reform until 1 January 2028, freezing the legal age at 62 years and 9 months and the contribution period at 170 quarters. The 2027 bill proposes freezing basic pensions in 2027 except the lowest.
items.claim: The suspension is a pause, not a repeal: the 2023 rules resume after 1 January 2028, and the 2027 freeze is part of the bill's savings.
items.assessment: Even after the under-indexation, pension benefits are one of the biggest spending increases in 2027 (+9 billion euros on the social-security field alone), behind interest costs.
items.status: Suspension in force until 1 January 2028; the 2027 freeze is in the PLFSS 2027 before Parliament.

items.name: Fiscal framework (LC 200/2023) and the 2027 primary target
items.what: Since 2023 federal policy runs on an annual primary-balance target with a tolerance band of 0.25 point of GDP either side, plus a cap on real primary-spending growth. For 2027 the target is a central-government surplus of 0.5% of GDP.
items.claim: The 2027 budget bill puts the result counted for the target at a surplus of R$83.4 billion (0.6% of GDP) after legal deductions, above the R$73.2 billion (0.5% of GDP) target, so the government says the framework is being met.
items.assessment: Formal compliance remains possible but rests on assumptions more optimistic than IFI's and a much thinner safety margin. In IFI's scenario the result counted for the target is a surplus of only R$0.9 billion, below even the lower tolerance bound, so about R$35.7 billion of discretionary spending would have to be frozen.
items.status: In force; the 2027 target is set in the budget guidelines bill (PLDO 2027).

items.name: 2027 budget bill (PLOA 2027)
items.what: The 2027 annual budget bill (PLN 24/2026), sent to Congress on 31 August 2026. Congress's joint budget committee amends it and both chambers vote it in December.
items.claim: An effective central-government primary surplus of R$18.6 billion (0.1% of GDP) in 2027, built on 2.5% GDP growth and 3.6% IPCA inflation.
items.assessment: Revenue could fall short if growth is below the 2.5% assumed, and assumed savings from benefit reviews may not materialise. IFI expects pension spending of R$1,239.2 billion against the bill's R$1,215.1 billion, part of a R$104.8 billion gap between the two projections of the effective result.

items.name: Consumption-tax reform (CBS and IBS)
items.what: Constitutional Amendment 132/2023 and Complementary Law 214/2025 replace federal and local consumption taxes with a dual VAT. The federal CBS replaces PIS and Cofins from 1 January 2027; the state and municipal IBS is phased in afterwards. The reference CBS rate is still to be set.
items.claim: The government projects R$636 billion of CBS revenue in 2027 in the budget bill; the law includes a mechanism to cut rates if the combined burden of the new taxes rises.
items.assessment: The 2027 bill adds a R$33.8 billion payment into the fund that compensates states for replacing IPI with the selective tax. It sits outside the LC 200 spending cap but counts towards the primary target, an example of how the transition's design adds fiscal pressure.
items.status: CBS starts on 1 January 2027; the Senate must set the reference rate by 15 December 2026.
items.next: Senate deadline to set the CBS reference rate

items.name: 2027 budget package (Paquete Económico 2027)
items.what: The 2027 economic package (general policy criteria, revenue law and spending budget) presented to the Chamber of Deputies on 8 September 2026.
items.claim: The broadest deficit measure (RFSP) falls from 4.1% of GDP in 2026 to 3.9% in 2027, with a primary surplus and debt (SHRFSP) at 55% of GDP; growth of 1.5% to 2.5% and inflation of 3.0% in 2027.
items.assessment: The package lowers the ambition of fiscal consolidation (3.9% against the 3.5% planned in April) and cuts the growth outlook. Private analysts surveyed by Banxico expect 1.8% growth; if growth undershoots, revenue would miss and push the deficit and debt up.
items.status: Before Congress; the Chamber must approve the spending budget by 15 November 2026.
items.next: Chamber of Deputies deadline to approve the 2027 spending budget (PEF)

items.name: Judicial reform and the second judicial election
items.what: The 2024 constitutional reform makes federal judges elected by popular vote; the first judicial election was held in June 2025. In May 2026 Congress approved moving the second judicial election from 2027 to June 2028.
items.claim: The government proposed the postponement so the judicial vote would not coincide with the June 2027 federal and state elections, citing the operational risks flagged by the electoral institute.
items.assessment: The reform creates important uncertainties about the effectiveness of contract enforcement and the predictability of the rule of law (2024 Article IV mission; not updated in the cited sources).
items.status: Second judicial election moved to June 2028 (approved by both chambers in May 2026, then sent to state legislatures).

items.name: Energy policy and support for Pemex
items.what: The 2025 energy laws give state firms Pemex and CFE priority. The Pemex Strategic Plan 2025-2035 (August 2025) and a Treasury capitalisation strategy aim to put Pemex's finances on a sustainable footing.
items.claim: The plan aims to make Pemex financially self-sufficient from 2027, no longer needing Treasury support.
items.assessment: The 2027 package still includes capital contributions to Pemex of 81.1 billion pesos (69.2% less than before), so the plan's original goal was not met. With losses of 28 billion pesos in the first half of 2026 and debt above US$77 billion, Pemex remains a risk to public finances.
items.status: In force; the 2027 contributions depend on the spending budget due by 15 November 2026.
items.next: Chamber of Deputies deadline to approve the 2027 spending budget (PEF)

items.name: IFI (Instituição Fiscal Independente, Federal Senate)
items.title: Relatório de Acompanhamento Fiscal – Out/2026
items.summary: The IFI expects a primary deficit of 0.5% of GDP in 2026 and a potential deficit of 1.0% of GDP in 2027, arguing that new spending commitments and lost revenue (about R$ 40 billion unbudgeted) call for a fiscal adjustment of roughly 3 percentage points of GDP. It also warns that the primary-result target misses large off-budget credit and fund operations, and that a higher neutral interest rate would raise the required primary surplus.

items.name: HCFP (Haut Conseil des finances publiques)
items.title: Avis n°2026 – 5 Lois de finances 2027
items.summary: The High Council of Public Finances judges the government's 2026 deficit forecast of 5.4% of GDP plausible, but considers the 2027 growth forecast of 1.0% optimistic and says risks to growth are mainly downward. It warns that the expected 2027 deficit reduction is too slow, that the debt-to-GDP ratio keeps rising toward about 122%, and that the 2029 target of a deficit below 3% of GDP is very unlikely to be met.

items.name: México Evalúa
items.title: El reto del Paquete Económico 2027: recuperar el margen para invertir en desarrollo
items.summary: México Evalúa finds that the 2027 Economic Package would lower the broad public deficit (RFSP) to 3.9% of GDP, a real improvement, but still above the 2.5% the IMF recommends, and that this effort is not enough to stabilize debt. The think tank warns that meeting the targets depends on record tax collection, a sharp cut in support for Pemex, and tight spending, with any shortfall likely falling on investment, health and education.

items.name: IMEF (Instituto Mexicano de Ejecutivos de Finanzas)
items.title: Información estratégica para líderes financieros: nuevo reporte IMEF
items.summary: The IMEF says Mexico's public finances are under pressure, with a broad public-sector deficit of 4.8% at the end of 2025, well above the 3.9% the government initially planned. It warns that high debt, continued support for Pemex and new labour costs bring Mexico closer to losing its investment-grade rating, and it expects weak growth of 1.3% in 2026.

The model predicts log returns; shown here as percentage changes. Out of sample it has been scored on 1 week so far.

em-macro: 5. Findings
items.text:
5. Findings — fit sample, 2005–2021

All files are in `results/fit/`. Moves are abnormal unless marked raw.

**Rate decisions.**

Currencies respond to the direction of the decision, but holds are non-events:

| FX, day 1 | n | mean % | t | variance ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| hikes | 137 | +0.56 | 4.1 | 2.0 |
| cuts | 227 | −0.17 | −1.9 | 1.4 |
| holds | 611 | −0.02 | −0.5 | 0.9 |

- **All decisions together:** the variance ratio is only 1.17. Most decisions are anticipated.
- **Surprises do move markets:**
  - **Brazil** (Focus, n=127): BRL gains 0.016% per bp of hawkish surprise on day 1 (t=1.9) and 0.028% by day 5
    (t=2.7). A 25bp surprise is worth about 0.4–0.7%.
  - **10y yields respond to surprises** in Mexico (+0.50bp per bp, t=6.1), Poland (+0.30, t=4.4) and South Africa
    (+0.28, t=2.4).
  - **Pooled across all countries** the FX effect is weak (t=1.3). Expectation coverage outside Brazil and Poland is
    thin and partly qualitative.
- **Long yields after hikes:** they fall 5bp on day 1 (curve flattening, t=−2.0), then rise 15bp by day 20 (t=2.8).

**Elections.**
- **Yields** move clearly. Day-1 10y yields fall 10.8bp on average (n=35, t=−2.6, z=−2.4), consistent with uncertainty
  resolving. General elections fall 17bp (t=−2.0), with a variance ratio of 4.
- **Currencies** on general elections (presidential and congressional votes together) have a day-1 variance ratio of
  2.2. They gain +2.1% by day 5 (n=12, t=4.7), but n is small.
- **Signed poll surprise:**
  - **FX:** +0.06% per pp, not significant in-sample (t=1.3, n=26).
  - **Yields:** −2.4bp per pp (t=−2.0, n=17). When the market-preferred side beats its polls, yields fall.
- **The size of the poll miss** does not predict the size of the move (|move| on |poll error|: t=−1.4).

**Drift vs reversal** (slope of day 1→5 on day 1; t in parentheses):

| | abnormal | raw | placebo days (raw) |
|---|---|---|---|
| FX, elections | −0.46 (−2.1) | −0.55 (−2.0) | 0.00 (0.0) |
| FX, rate decisions | −0.25 (−3.9) | −0.08 (−1.2) | — |
| 10y, elections | +0.47 (3.1) | +0.39 (2.7) | +0.15 (1.7) |
| 10y, rate decisions | +0.06 (0.7) | +0.13 (1.5) | — |

- **Rate decisions:** the apparent FX reversal is mostly an artefact of the factor adjustment, mixing noon-NY FX with
  end-of-day US factors. On raw moves it is small and insignificant, and placebo days show the same adjusted pattern
  (−0.06 at h=5, −0.26 at h=20).
- **Elections:** in-sample, currencies **reverse** part of their day-1 move. Bond moves **continue**.

Applying the pre-registered fade-the-day-1-move rule to elections in-sample earns +1.0% a year with a Sharpe of 0.23
(50 trades). That beats in-sample carry (Sharpe 0.06), but the rule was chosen on the same data.

items.title: em-macro: 6. Hold-out
items.text:
6. Hold-out, 2022 to Oct 2026 — evaluated once

All files are in `results/test/`.

**Trading rule vs carry** (`strategy_vs_carry.csv`, monthly, 2022-01 to 2026-09):

| | ann. return % | Sharpe | max DD % | trades | hit rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| carry basket (the bar) | +2.6 | 0.46 | −10.1 | — | — |
| fade election day-1 move, hold to day 5 | −3.3 | −1.00 | −15.7 | 14 | 29% |
| fade election day-1 move, hold to day 20 | −4.8 | −0.53 | −26.2 | 14 | 43% |

**The rule fails.** Hold-out election FX moves *continued* rather than reversed: the raw slope is +0.46 (t=1.7, n=14).
It lost on Brazil's 2022 run-off, Turkey's 2023 run-off and Mexico's 2024 election. The in-sample reversal is best
read as a small-sample artefact, not a tradeable effect.

**What did hold up** (`oos_surprise_predictions.csv`):
- **Poll surprise and day-1 FX moves:** the frozen fit-sample regression predicts the hold-out moves with a
  correlation of 0.72, the right sign in 8 of 9 elections, and an out-of-sample R² of 0.15 against a zero forecast.
  The cases are Brazil 2022 and 2026, Poland 2023 and 2025, Turkey 2023 and Indonesia 2024 (chart below).
- **But the fitted slope was not significant in-sample**, and 9 events is very few. Treat this as consistent evidence,
  not proof.
- **The bond-yield surprise regression did not hold up** (R² ≈ 0, correlation −0.17).
- **The rate-surprise regressions add almost nothing out of sample** (pooled FX correlation 0.18, R² 0.02).
- **Rate decisions overall:** hold-out decisions are even quieter than in-sample. The FX variance ratio is 0.82, hikes
  average +0.15% with t=0.9, and the FX drift slopes are insignificant.



**The biggest hold-out events:**
- **Brazil, 2-Oct-2022, first round:** Bolsonaro beat his polls by 7.8pp. BRL +4.1% abnormal on day 1, 10y −31bp.
- **Brazil, 4-Oct-2026, first round:** BRL +4.8%, 10y −120bp.
- **Brazil, 25-Oct-2026, run-off:** Lula beat odds that gave Flávio Bolsonaro 80%. The 10y rose +255bp on day 1. The
  FX move is outside the study because FRED's BRL ends on 23-Oct, but BCB PTAX shows BRL −8.4%.
- **Turkey, 14-May-2023:** the 10y fell 298bp on day 1 and 533bp by day 5.
- **Mexico, 2-Jun-2024:** MXN −3.5% on day 1 and −7.2% by day 5. Note this is *not* a poll miss on the presidency
  (Sheinbaum led by 17pp and won by 33pp). The worry was Morena's congressional supermajority, which a two-candidate
  margin cannot capture.

items.title: em-macro: One-time test, 2020 onward
items.text:
One-time test, 2020 onward (`results/risk_model/test/`, v1 as specified)

The forecast of each spread change is −κ × gap. It is compared with "no change" by RMSE ratio (below 1 means the
model is better) and a Diebold–Mariano t-statistic (positive means better), and also after dropping the five
largest moves.

| v1 spread mispricing | 3 months: RMSE ratio (DM t) | without top-5 moves | 6 months: RMSE ratio (DM t) | without top-5 moves |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| all 12 countries | 1.00 (−0.2) | 1.01 (−0.5) | 0.98 (0.6) | 1.01 (−0.4) |
| **Brazil** | 0.99 (1.1) | 0.99 (1.1) | 0.98 (0.5) | 0.97 (0.9) |
| **Mexico** | 0.99 (0.9) | 0.99 (0.7) | 0.98 (0.6) | 1.00 (0.0) |
| **France** | 1.59 (−3.3) | 1.72 (−3.4) | 2.34 (−3.6) | 2.44 (−3.5) |

- **Brazil and Mexico:** at best 1–3% better than no change, not significant.
- **France:** far worse. Its spread kept widening in 2024–26 while the v1 model put its fair value far below.
- **The 6-month pooled edge (0.98)** disappears once the five largest moves are removed.
- **Other countries:** the only ones with a gain of 5% or more are South Africa (0.88 at 6 months, DM 1.7) and
  Indonesia (0.92). Spain and France are clearly worse.
- **Currency mispricing** is worse than no change (pooled 1.04 and 1.10). Mexico is 0.95–0.99; Brazil is 1.09–1.29.

**v2** (`results/risk_model/test_v2_posthoc/`) — **post-hoc: chosen after the 2020+ test; not a clean out-of-sample result**:

| | 3 months | 6 months |
|---|---|---|
| pooled | 1.00 (DM −0.3) | 0.98 (DM 0.3) |
| pooled, without top-5 moves | 1.01 | 1.02 |
| Brazil | 0.98 | 0.97 |
| Mexico | 0.99 | 0.97 |
| France | 1.08 | 1.18 |

v2 fixes France's level problem but does not create forecasting power.

**Conclusion: no version of the mispricing signal beats no-change out of sample, and nothing survives removing the
largest moves.**

items.name: France
items.structure: Euro-area sovereign with no currency of its own; the ECB sets policy for the whole area and its Transmission Protection Instrument is conditional on fiscal compliance. Ratings sit in the AA/A band, and losing the last AA-category rating matters for some reserve managers.
items.politics: Minority government since the 2024 dissolution. Budgets pass either by vote or by Article 49.3, which exposes the government to a censure motion. If no budget is adopted in time, Article 47 lets the government act by ordinance after the parliamentary deadline, and a special law can roll over taxes and spending into the new year. The next presidential election is in spring 2027.
items.where_consensus_errs: Rating-agency timing (scheduled review dates are published, but agencies can affirm while moving the outlook), the gap between official deficit targets and independent estimates, and the speed at which a censure vote turns into a market move.

items.name: Brazil
items.instruments: USD/BRL (primary); DI futures and long Tesouro bonds (context).
items.structure: Inflation-targeting central bank (Copom meets eight times a year). Fiscal policy runs under the LC 200/2023 framework: a primary-balance target with a tolerance band and a cap on real spending growth. The Focus survey gives weekly market expectations and their dispersion.
items.politics: A new government term starts in January 2027 after the October 2026 elections. Fiscal credibility hinges on whether the framework is kept, loosened through exclusions, or rewritten.
items.where_consensus_errs: Official fiscal targets versus Focus estimates, and Copom surprises, which em-macro found move the real within days when the Focus dispersion is high.

items.name: Mexico
items.structure: Inflation-targeting central bank (Banxico). Investment-grade sovereign whose index eligibility depends on the middle of the three agency ratings; Pemex's support is a recurring fiscal burden.
items.politics: Morena and its allies govern; the June 2027 midterms decide whether they keep the two-thirds majority needed to amend the constitution alone. Trade policy is tied to the USMCA joint review due in July 2027.
items.where_consensus_errs: Congressional supermajorities that a two-candidate poll margin cannot capture (the 2024 case in em-macro), and US trade decisions that arrive outside the scheduled calendar.

items.name: United States
items.instruments: US 10-year Treasury yield and the broad dollar (global backdrop only).
items.structure: The global rates and dollar backdrop for all three countries. USTR leads the USMCA review.
items.where_consensus_errs: Tariff and trade announcements that are not on any calendar.
